title: Semisimple centralizers in smooth connected solvable groups are connected
statement: Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field [def-weil-field, def-weil-algebraic-closure]. All groups below are affine group schemes [def-sc-group-scheme] of finite type [def-weil-finite-type-morphism] over $k$, and all subgroups are closed subgroup schemes [def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup]. Smoothness and connectedness have the meanings of [def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme]. Let $G$ be smooth, connected and solvable, where solvable means that its successive scheme-theoretic commutator subgroup schemes eventually become trivial. A point $s\in G(k)$ is semisimple if its image in every finite-dimensional algebraic representation $G\to\operatorname{GL}(V)$ is diagonalizable; here $V$ is a finite-dimensional $k$-vector space, $\operatorname{GL}(V)$ is its group scheme of invertible linear maps, and an algebraic representation is a homomorphism of group schemes. For a semisimple point $s\in G(k)$, let $C_G(s)$ be the closed subscheme of $G$ defined by equality of the morphisms $g\mapsto gs$ and $g\mapsto sg$, so that $C_G(s)(A)=\{g\in G(A):gs_A=s_Ag\}$ for each commutative $k$-algebra $A$ [def-weil-closed-immersion, def-pc-fibre-product]. Then $C_G(s)$ is connected.

source.place: Theorem 16.40, printed pp.338–339, connectedness assertion; the proof is induction using Lemma 16.39 and the quotient sequence. The extra unipotent-factor assertion of the theorem is not needed.

proof.text: Write $G^{(0)}=G$ and $G^{(i+1)}=D_{G^{(i)}}$, where $D_H$ is the smallest closed subgroup through which the commutator morphism of $H$ factors. Use strong induction on the least $d\geq0$ with $G^{(d)}=1$, simultaneously for all smooth connected solvable affine groups over $k$ and all their semisimple points. If $G$ is commutative (including the trivial group, $d=0$), both defining morphisms of $C_G(s)$ agree on every algebra, so $C_G(s)=G$ and the assertion is the assumed connectedness of $G$. Otherwise $d\geq2$.

source.place: Theorem 16.40, printed p.339, induction and commutative base case; induction is indexed by derived length instead of dimension.

proof.text: Repeated application of [lem-sfb-smooth-connected-derived-subgroup] shows that every $G^{(i)}$ is smooth and connected. Its minimal commutator-subgroup description is preserved by every automorphism: applying an automorphism and its inverse gives the two inclusions. Recursively, conjugation by each $g\in G(k)$ preserves every $G^{(i)}$ as a subgroup scheme. Since $G$ is smooth, [lem-sfb-smooth-ambient-normality-geometric] makes each $G^{(i)}$ normal in $G$. Put $N=G^{(d-1)}$. It is nontrivial, smooth, connected and commutative, the last assertion because its commutator subgroup is $1$. The derived series itself is a solvable series as required by [lem-sfb-lie-kolchin-triangular-embedding]: the quotient by each successor is commutative, since quotient sections locally lift and their commutators map to $1$. Embed $G$ into $B_n$ using that node. The diagonal of every upper-triangular commutator is $1$, on every algebra, so the minimality of $G^{(1)}$ puts it inside $U_n$. Consequently $N\subseteq G^{(1)}\subseteq U_n$ is unipotent.

source.place: Theorem 16.40, first paragraph of proof, p.339; Theorem 16.30 (Lie–Kolchin), pp.335–336; derived subgroups as in Section 6(e). Quotient local lifting is Theorem 5.28.

proof.text: By [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry], form the faithfully flat quotient $q:G\to Q=G/N$; $Q$ is smooth, connected, affine and of finite type. Connectedness over the algebraically closed base is the geometric connectedness required there. The same node gives the closed subgroups $Q_i=G^{(i)}/N$ for $0\leq i\leq d-1$ and their successive quotients $Q_i/Q_{i+1}\simeq G^{(i)}/G^{(i+1)}$. Each such quotient is commutative: commutators of local lifts from $G^{(i)}$ land in $G^{(i+1)}$. Thus, by the defining minimality of the derived subgroup, $D(Q_i)\subseteq Q_{i+1}$, and recursively $Q^{(i)}\subseteq Q_i$. In particular $Q^{(d-1)}=1$. This proves both solvability and the strict decrease of the induction index, without assuming that quotient maps are surjective on all algebras. The point $\bar s=q(s)$ is semisimple because every representation of $Q$ pulls back to a representation of $G$. The induction hypothesis now gives connectedness of $D=C_Q(\bar s)$.

source.place: Theorem 16.40, quotient and induction paragraph, p.339; Theorems 5.28 and 5.55 for the quotient series.

proof.text: Set $C=C_G(s)$ and $K=C_N(s)$. Apply [lem-sfb-semisimple-fixed-subscheme-smooth] to the conjugation actions of the smooth connected group $G$ on the smooth affine schemes $G$, $N$, and $Q$, where the last action is through $q$. Their fixed schemes for $s$ are respectively $C$, $K$, and $D$. Therefore all three are smooth. This uses the represented equalizers on every algebra, including nonreduced algebras. Apply [lem-sfb-semisimple-commutative-unipotent-commutator] to $N\triangleleft G$ and $s$; all its hypotheses were established in step 2. It gives that $K$ is connected and the decomposition used in the next step.

source.place: Corollary 13.8, p.257, and Lemma 16.39, p.338, as used in Theorem 16.40.

proof.text:
Fix $y\in D(k)$. Apply [lem-sfb-affine-group-homomorphism-image] to the faithfully flat map $q$ with smooth target $Q$: choose $z\in G(k)$ with $q(z)=y$. Since $y$ centralizes $\bar s$, the commutator $x=[s,z]$ belongs to $N(k)$. By [lem-sfb-semisimple-commutative-unipotent-commutator] write $[s,z]=[s,u]v$ with $u\in N(k)$ and $v\in K(k)$. Expanding commutators and using the commutativity of $N$ gives
$$z s^{-1}z^{-1}=u s^{-1}u^{-1}v.$$
The element $v$ commutes with $u$ because both lie in $N(k)$, and with $s$ because $v\in K(k)$. It therefore commutes with $u s^{-1}u^{-1}$.

source.place: Theorem 16.40, middle paragraph, p.339; Lemma 16.39, p.338; rational-point lifting is Summary 1.71.

proof.text: Use the faithful triangular representation from step 2. The matrices of $z s^{-1}z^{-1}$ and $u s^{-1}u^{-1}$ are diagonalizable: the inverse of a diagonalizable matrix is diagonalizable, and conjugation just changes its eigenbasis. The matrix of $v$ is unipotent, since $v\in N(k)\subseteq U_n(k)$, and it commutes with the second matrix. Thus the displayed equality in step 5 gives a semisimple-unipotent decomposition of its left side. By uniqueness in [lem-sfb-multiplicative-jordan-linear-compatibility], the unipotent matrix is the identity. Faithfulness gives $v=1$. Hence $[s,z]=[s,u]$, and direct cancellation gives $s(u^{-1}z)s^{-1}=u^{-1}z$. Also $q(u^{-1}z)=y$ because $u\in N(k)$. We have produced a point of $C(k)$ above every $y\in D(k)$.

source.place: Theorem 16.40, Jordan-decomposition calculation, p.339; multiplicative Jordan uniqueness is Section 9(c).

proof.text: The restriction $f:C\to D$ of $q$ is a group homomorphism. It is defined on every algebra because $q(cs)=q(sc)$ for $c\in C(A)$. Its scheme-theoretic kernel is $K$: on each commutative $k$-algebra $A$, its kernel consists precisely of points of $N(A)$ commuting with $s_A$. Thus $K$ is normal in $C$. Both $C,D$ are affine finite-type groups and $D$ is smooth by step 4; the surjectivity on $k$-points proved in steps 5–6 therefore makes $f$ faithfully flat by [lem-sfb-affine-group-homomorphism-image].

source.place: Theorem 16.40, exact sequence, p.339; Summary 1.71, p.28.

proof.text: Form $\pi:C\to R=C/K$ by [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry]. Since $f$ kills $K$ on every algebra, the quotient sheaf property gives a homomorphism $h:R\to D$ with $h\pi=f$. Conversely [lem-sfb-faithfully-flat-group-quotient-universal] applied to $f$ and the map $\pi$ gives $j:D\to R$ with $jf=\pi$. Uniqueness in the same universal property, applied first to $f$ and then to $\pi$, yields $hj=1_D$ and $jh=1_R$. Hence $R\simeq D$ is smooth and connected by steps 3–4. Now apply the inverse-image connectedness clause of [lem-sfb-affine-normal-quotient-geometry] to $\pi$, its smooth connected kernel $K$, and the whole subgroup $S=R\subseteq R$. Its inverse image is $C$, so $C$ is connected. This completes the induction.

source.place: Theorem 16.40, final connectedness inference, p.339; Proposition 5.59(a), p.114, as included in the quotient-geometry node, and quotient universal property (5.28, 5.79).

proof_origin.place: Theorem 16.40, pp.338–339, connectedness proof via Lemma 16.39. Same last-derived-subgroup induction indexed by derived length; auxiliary smoothness from Corollary 13.8.
